steps.overview: This step sets up a clean Python environment for agent work and makes your first chat model call with LangChain v1. Every later step (LangGraph, LangSmith, Langflow) assumes you can create an isolated environment, load API keys safely from the environment, and call a model both synchronously and with asyncio. Getting this right early prevents leaked keys, version conflicts and confusing import errors.
objectives: Create an isolated Python 3.10+ environment with venv or uv and install langchain plus a provider package.
Store API keys in a .env file, keep it out of Git, and load them into the environment with python-dotenv.
Call a chat model from a script using init_chat_model or a provider class, and print the response content.
Use asyncio.run with ainvoke to make asynchronous model calls and run several calls concurrently.
Diagnose common setup errors such as a missing provider package, an inactive environment or an unset key.

concepts.explanation: LangChain v1 and current LangGraph releases need Python 3.10 or newer. Check with `python --version` before you install anything. Older interpreters cause install failures or missing features, so fix the interpreter first.

A venv is a per-project folder, usually .venv, with its own interpreter and installed packages. Create it with `python -m venv .venv` and activate it before installing. This keeps LangChain versions in one project from breaking another.

uv is a fast Python package and project manager from Astral. `uv venv` creates the environment, `uv add <pkg>` adds a dependency to pyproject.toml and installs it, and `uv run script.py` runs the script inside the project environment. It replaces pip and venv for most workflows and is much faster.

The `langchain` package gives you the core abstractions and create_agent. The model integrations ship separately, for example `langchain-anthropic` or `langchain-openai`. You must install the provider package for the model you call, or imports and init_chat_model will fail.

A .env file holds KEY=value lines such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... . `load_dotenv()` from python-dotenv copies them into os.environ at startup. Provider classes then read the standard variable name automatically, so the key never appears in code.

`from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model` builds a chat model from a string such as "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5". It gives one provider-agnostic way to create models, and the same string format is accepted by create_agent later. Call `.invoke(...)` on the result to get an AIMessage.

A chat model call returns an AIMessage object, not a plain string. The reply is in `.content`, and token counts are in `.usage_metadata` when the provider reports them. Printing the whole object shows metadata; printing `.content` shows the answer.

LangChain runnables have async twins: ainvoke, abatch and astream. You define `async def main()`, `await model.ainvoke(...)`, and start the program with `asyncio.run(main())`. Use `asyncio.gather` to run several model calls concurrently, because waiting on network I/O is where async saves time.

keyFacts: LangChain v1 requires Python 3.10 or newer.
Create and activate a venv: `python -m venv .venv`, then `source .venv/bin/activate` (macOS/Linux) or `.venv\Scripts\activate` (Windows).
Install the core library plus one provider: `pip install -U langchain langchain-anthropic python-dotenv`.
Standard key variable names: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for Anthropic and OPENAI_API_KEY for OpenAI; provider classes read them automatically.
LangSmith tracing later uses LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY; put them in the same .env file.
Add .env to .gitignore and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.
By default, load_dotenv() does not overwrite variables that already exist in the environment; pass override=True only if you want the file to win.
`asyncio.run()` starts the event loop once at the entry point; do not call it from inside an already running loop such as a Jupyter cell, where you use `await` directly.
A model call returns an AIMessage; the text is in `.content`.

example.caption: first_call.py: load keys from .env, then make a sync and an async call (run with `python first_call.py` or `uv run first_call.py`)
example.code:
import asyncio
import os

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

load_dotenv()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from .env into os.environ

if not os.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"):
    raise RuntimeError("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set. Add it to .env")

model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", temperature=0)

# Synchronous call
reply = model.invoke("Explain a Python virtual environment in one sentence.")
print("SYNC:", reply.content)


# Asynchronous calls, run concurrently
async def main() -> None:
    questions = ["What is asyncio?", "What is a .env file?"]
    replies = await asyncio.gather(*(model.ainvoke(q) for q in questions))
    for q, r in zip(questions, replies):
        print(f"ASYNC {q} -> {r.content}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

pitfalls: Hard-coding the key, for example `ChatAnthropic(api_key="sk-...")`, and pushing it to GitHub. Keys in Git history stay exposed; rotate any leaked key immediately.
Installing only `langchain` and then getting an import or provider error. You also need the provider package such as langchain-anthropic.
Installing packages into the global Python because the venv was not activated. Check with `which python` or `where python`, or use `uv run`.
Printing the AIMessage object and thinking the call failed or returned noise. Print `reply.content` for the text.
Calling `asyncio.run()` inside Jupyter, which already runs an event loop and raises an error. Use `await model.ainvoke(...)` directly in the cell.
Following old tutorials that use removed or legacy APIs such as LLMChain or initialize_agent. In v1, call models directly and build agents with create_agent from langchain.agents.

files.code:
# hello-chat-model

Step 1 of the Agentic AI with Python track: call a chat model from a script.

## What you learn
- Python 3.10+ in an isolated environment (uv or venv)
- API keys in a `.env` file, loaded with python-dotenv (never hard-coded)
- `langchain` plus one provider package (`langchain-anthropic` or `langchain-openai`)
- `init_chat_model` returns a chat model; `invoke` returns an `AIMessage`
- `asyncio` with `ainvoke` to run several calls concurrently

## Setup with uv (recommended)
```bash
uv sync                      # creates .venv and installs pyproject deps
cp .env.example .env         # edit .env and add your key
uv run python hello_model.py
uv run python async_hello.py "What is a virtual environment?"
```

## Setup with venv and pip
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install langchain langchain-anthropic langchain-openai python-dotenv
python hello_model.py
```

## Choosing a model
Set `MODEL` in `.env` as `provider:model-name`, for example
`anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5` or `openai:gpt-4.1-mini`.
You only need the key for the provider you use.

## Checkpoint
- `grep -rn "sk-" *.py` finds nothing: no key is in the code.
- Delete the key from `.env` and run again: `config.py` stops with a clear error.
- `.env` is listed in `.gitignore`, so it is never committed.

# Project metadata read by uv (uv sync / uv run).
[project]
name = "hello-chat-model"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Step 1: call a chat model from a Python script"
readme = "README.md"
# LangChain v1 needs Python 3.10 or newer
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "langchain>=1.0",            # core package: init_chat_model, messages
    "langchain-anthropic>=1.0",  # provider package for Claude models
    "langchain-openai>=1.0",     # provider package for OpenAI models
    "python-dotenv>=1.0",        # loads .env into os.environ
]

# No [build-system]: uv treats this as an application, not a library.

# Copy to .env and fill in real values. Never commit .env.

# Model in provider:model-name form, read by config.py
MODEL=anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5

# Provider keys: set the one that matches MODEL
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
OPENAI_API_KEY=

# Optional: LangSmith tracing (used from Step 4 onwards)
LANGSMITH_TRACING=false
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=

# Secrets: real keys live only here
.env

# Virtual environments created by uv or venv
.venv/
venv/

# Python cache files
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# uv lock file is safe to commit; keep it tracked
# uv.lock

"""Load settings from the environment and build the chat model."""
import os
import sys

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

# Read .env into os.environ. Real environment variables win over .env.
load_dotenv()

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5")

# Which environment variable each provider package reads its key from
KEY_VARS = {
    "anthropic": "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY",
    "openai": "OPENAI_API_KEY",
}


def check_key() -> None:
    """Fail early with a clear message if the provider key is missing."""
    provider = MODEL.split(":", 1)[0]
    key_var = KEY_VARS.get(provider)
    if key_var is None:
        sys.exit(f"Unknown provider '{provider}' in MODEL={MODEL}")
    if not os.getenv(key_var):
        sys.exit(f"{key_var} is not set. Add it to your .env file.")


def get_model():
    """Return a chat model. The key is read from the environment, not passed here."""
    check_key()
    # init_chat_model picks the provider package from the 'provider:' prefix
    return init_chat_model(MODEL, temperature=0, max_tokens=300)

"""Hands-on task: call a chat model from a script and print the response."""
from langchain.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage

from config import MODEL, get_model


def main() -> None:
    model = get_model()

    messages = [
        SystemMessage("You are a concise Python tutor. Answer in 2 sentences."),
        HumanMessage("Why should I use a virtual environment for AI projects?"),
    ]

    # invoke is the synchronous call; it returns an AIMessage
    reply = model.invoke(messages)

    print(f"Model: {MODEL}")
    print(f"Type : {type(reply).__name__}")  # AIMessage
    print("Reply:")
    print(reply.content)  # the text of the answer

    # Token counts, standardised across providers (may be None for some)
    print("Usage:", reply.usage_metadata)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Async basics: run several model calls at the same time with ainvoke."""
import asyncio
import sys
import time

from config import get_model

QUESTIONS = [
    "What is uv in one sentence?",
    "What does python-dotenv do in one sentence?",
    "What is asyncio in one sentence?",
]


async def ask(model, question: str) -> str:
    # ainvoke is the async twin of invoke; await it inside a coroutine
    reply = await model.ainvoke(question)
    return f"Q: {question}\nA: {reply.content}\n"


async def main() -> None:
    model = get_model()
    # Optional extra question from the command line
    questions = QUESTIONS + sys.argv[1:]

    start = time.perf_counter()
    # gather runs all calls concurrently and keeps the input order
    answers = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(model, q) for q in questions))
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    for text in answers:
        print(text)
    print(f"{len(questions)} calls finished in {elapsed:.1f}s (concurrently)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # asyncio.run starts the event loop and runs main() to completion
    asyncio.run(main())

revision.examFocus: There is no proctored exam for this step. LangChain Academy courses are free and self-paced, and Langflow has no certification. This step is the prerequisite for every notebook in the LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith courses, and interviewers test it through quick practical questions. Typical questions are: why did the import fail, where should the key live, why did asyncio.run crash in Jupyter, and why did print show an object instead of text.

compare.difference: venv is built into Python and needs manual activation before pip installs. uv is a separate, fast tool that creates and uses the project environment for you through `uv run` or `uv add`, so there is no activation step to forget.
compare.chooseA: Pick venv when the setup must use only the standard library, or when a course notebook gives pip commands.
compare.chooseB: Pick uv when you want fast, reproducible installs and want to avoid the 'forgot to activate, installed globally' mistake.

compare.difference: The default keeps any variable already set in the shell or CI. override=True lets the .env file replace it.
compare.chooseA: Use the default in most cases, so a production or CI secret is not silently replaced by a local file.
compare.chooseB: Use override=True only when a stale shell variable is shadowing the key you just changed in .env.

compare.difference: invoke is synchronous and blocks until the reply arrives. ainvoke is a coroutine that needs an event loop and lets several calls overlap.
compare.chooseA: Use invoke for a simple script, or for one call at a time.
compare.chooseB: Use ainvoke for web servers, concurrent calls with asyncio.gather, or inside Jupyter with top-level await.

compare.difference: asyncio.run creates a new event loop and fails if a loop is already running. Bare await only works where a loop already exists.
compare.chooseA: Use asyncio.run once, at the entry point of a .py script.
compare.chooseB: Use bare await in a Jupyter or IPython cell, or inside another async function.

compare.difference: init_chat_model is a provider-agnostic factory, so you can switch models by changing a string. The provider class gives direct access to provider-specific parameters. Both still need the provider package installed.
compare.chooseA: Pick init_chat_model when the question stresses swapping providers or keeping code model-agnostic.
compare.chooseB: Pick the provider class when you need a provider-specific setting or explicit typed construction.

cues.cue: ImportError or 'unable to infer model provider' right after pip install langchain
cues.pick: Install the provider package, for example langchain-anthropic or langchain-openai.
cues.why: The core langchain package does not ship provider integrations.

cues.cue: Key accidentally pushed to GitHub
cues.pick: Rotate or revoke the key at the provider first, then clean up the repo.
cues.why: Deleting the file does not remove it from Git history, and bots scan public repos within minutes.

cues.cue: 'asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop'
cues.pick: Use await directly in the notebook cell.
cues.why: Jupyter already runs an event loop.

cues.cue: Package installed but 'ModuleNotFoundError' when running the script
cues.pick: Activate the venv, or run with uv run, and check the interpreter with which python or where python.
cues.why: The package went into a different interpreter from the one running the script.

cues.cue: print(reply) shows content=... with metadata
cues.pick: Print reply.content.
cues.why: The call succeeded; the reply is an AIMessage object, not a plain string.

cues.cue: Tutorial uses LLMChain or initialize_agent
cues.pick: Call the model directly, and use create_agent from langchain.agents for agents.
cues.why: These are legacy APIs that LangChain v1 does not use.

cues.cue: Changed the key in .env but the old key is still used
cues.pick: Check for an exported shell variable, or use override=True.
cues.why: By default load_dotenv does not overwrite existing variables.

cues.cue: Share config with teammates without sharing secrets
cues.pick: Commit a .env.example with empty values and keep .env in .gitignore.
cues.why: It documents the required variable names without exposing any values.

scenario.situation: A learner clones a course repo and runs `pip install langchain` in a new terminal. They paste their Anthropic key into `ChatAnthropic(api_key=...)` and run the script. They get a ModuleNotFoundError for langchain_anthropic, and later push the code to GitHub. What is the correct set of fixes?
reasoning: The missing module tells you the provider package was never installed. The core langchain package alone is not enough.
A new terminal means the venv may not be active, so check the interpreter before installing anything.
The pasted key is now in Git history. Rotation is required, not optional, and editing the file does not undo the exposure.
Reject answers that only delete the line, only make the repo private, or only add .gitignore after the fact. None of these protects the leaked key.
scenario.answer: Rotate the leaked key immediately. Activate the venv (or use uv) and install langchain, langchain-anthropic and python-dotenv. Move the key to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a git-ignored .env file, loaded with load_dotenv(), so the provider class reads it automatically.

memoryAids: V-I-K-R: Venv on, Install core + provider, Keys in .env, Read .content.
Script runs the loop (asyncio.run); a notebook already has one (just await).
Leaked key? Rotate first, clean up later. History never forgets.
cheatSheet: LangChain v1 needs Python 3.10 or newer; check with python --version inside the active environment.
One environment per project: python -m venv .venv, then activate it, or let uv manage it.
Install the core and a provider together: langchain plus langchain-anthropic or langchain-openai, plus python-dotenv.
Use the standard variable names ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY; provider classes read them without any api_key argument.
Add LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY to the same .env now, so tracing works in later steps.
Call load_dotenv() before you create the model, otherwise the key is not yet in os.environ.
Keep .env in .gitignore and commit .env.example with blank values.
Use init_chat_model with a provider:model string for swappable models.
A reply is an AIMessage; use .content for the text, and note it can be a list of blocks for some providers.
Use invoke in scripts, ainvoke for concurrency, and asyncio.gather to run several ainvoke calls at once.
Use asyncio.run only at the script entry point, never inside Jupyter.
Ignore LLMChain and initialize_agent; v1 agents use create_agent from langchain.agents.
selfCheck: I can create and activate a venv on my OS, or use uv run, and prove which interpreter is active.
I can install the correct packages and explain why the core langchain package alone causes a provider error.
I can load keys from a git-ignored .env file and explain when override=True changes the result.
I can call a chat model synchronously and asynchronously, and print only the reply text.
I can explain why asyncio.run fails in Jupyter and write the correct cell code instead.
I can describe the exact response steps when an API key is leaked to a public repo.

objective.question: You are setting up a new machine for a LangChain v1 project. Which Python version meets the minimum requirement?
options: Python 3.9
Any Python 3.x release
Python 3.10 or newer
Python 3.8
objective.explanation: LangChain v1 requires Python 3.10 or newer. Python 3.8 and 3.9 are below the minimum, so 'any Python 3.x' is also wrong.

objective.question: On Windows, you ran `python -m venv .venv` in your project folder. Which command activates this environment in Command Prompt?
options: ./.venv/bin/python activate
activate .venv
\.venv\Scripts\activate
source .venv/bin/activate
objective.explanation: On Windows the activation script is in .venv\Scripts\activate. `source .venv/bin/activate` is the macOS/Linux form, and the other two are not valid activation commands.

objective.question: You want to call Claude models from LangChain and load keys from a .env file. Which single install command covers all three needs?
options: pip install -U langchain langchain-anthropic python-dotenv
pip install -U langchain-core langsmith
pip install -U anthropic dotenv
pip install -U langchain
objective.explanation: You need the core langchain library, the provider package langchain-anthropic, and python-dotenv for .env loading. The other options miss the provider package, the dotenv loader, or both.

objective.question: A teammate writes `ChatAnthropic(model=..., api_key="sk-ant-...")` directly in main.py. What is the best fix that also passes the step checkpoint?
options: Put ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env, add .env to .gitignore, call load_dotenv(), and remove the api_key argument
Encode the key in base64 inside the script
Store the key in a constants.py file that is committed to Git
Move the key to a comment at the top of the file
objective.explanation: Provider classes read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment automatically, so loading it from a git-ignored .env removes the hard-coded secret. Comments, base64 and committed constants files all still leak the key.

objective.question: Your shell already has OPENAI_API_KEY set to an old value. Your .env file has a new value. You call `load_dotenv()` with no arguments. Which key does your script use?
options: The old value already in the shell environment
Neither; load_dotenv raises a conflict error
Both values joined together
The new value from .env
objective.explanation: By default load_dotenv() does not overwrite variables that already exist in the environment, so the shell value wins. You must pass override=True for the .env file to take priority.

objective.question: What should you commit to Git so that teammates know which environment variables the project needs?
options: A .env.example file listing the variable names with empty values
Nothing; variable names must stay secret
A screenshot of your terminal with the keys
The real .env file
objective.explanation: A .env.example with empty values documents the required names without exposing secrets. The real .env must stay in .gitignore, and variable names themselves are not secret.

objective.question: You run `response = model.invoke("Say hello")`. What type is `response`, and where is the generated text?
options: An AIMessage; read response.content
A HumanMessage; read response.message
A dict; read response['text']
A plain str; print it directly
objective.explanation: A chat model call returns an AIMessage, and the model's text is in its .content attribute. It is not a plain string, a dict or a HumanMessage.

objective.question: In a Jupyter notebook cell you write `asyncio.run(main())` and get a RuntimeError about a running event loop. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace it with `await main()` directly in the cell
Change ainvoke to invoke inside main()
Wrap the call in a try/except and ignore the error
Restart the kernel and run the same line again
objective.explanation: Jupyter already runs an event loop, and asyncio.run() cannot start a second one inside it. You use `await main()` directly in the cell. Restarting or ignoring the error does not fix the cause, and switching to invoke just gives up on async.

objective.question: Which snippet correctly makes an asynchronous model call in a standalone script?
options:
def main():
    r = await model.ainvoke("Hi")
    print(r.content)
main()

async def main():
    r = await model.invoke("Hi")
    print(r.content)
main()

async def main():
    r = await model.ainvoke("Hi")
    print(r.content)
asyncio.run(main())

async def main():
    r = model.ainvoke("Hi")
    print(r.content)
asyncio.run(main())
objective.explanation: ainvoke is a coroutine, so you must await it inside an async function, and asyncio.run() starts the loop at the entry point. The other options forget await, use await outside an async def, await the sync invoke, or never start the loop.

objective.question: You need to send five independent prompts to a model and want them to run concurrently in one script. Which approach fits best?
options: Use await asyncio.gather(*(model.ainvoke(p) for p in prompts)) inside one async main
Create five separate virtual environments
Call model.invoke() five times inside an async function
Call asyncio.run() once per prompt in a for loop
objective.explanation: asyncio.gather runs several ainvoke coroutines concurrently inside one event loop started by a single asyncio.run(). Repeated asyncio.run() calls run one after another, and sync invoke blocks the loop.

objective.question: You want your code to switch between Anthropic and OpenAI by changing only a model string. Which LangChain helper is designed for this?
options: load_dotenv from dotenv
InMemorySaver from langgraph
create_agent from langchain.agents
init_chat_model from langchain.chat_models
objective.explanation: init_chat_model creates a chat model from a provider and model name, for example a 'provider:model' string, so switching providers is a one-line change if the provider package is installed. load_dotenv loads variables, create_agent builds agents, and InMemorySaver is a checkpointer.

objective.question: Later in the course you will enable LangSmith tracing. Where and how should those settings go?
options: Put them in requirements.txt
Pass them as arguments to init_chat_model
Add LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY to the same git-ignored .env file
Hard-code them in every script that calls a model
objective.explanation: LangSmith reads LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY from the environment, so they belong in the same .env file as your provider keys. Hard-coding leaks secrets, and requirements.txt and init_chat_model are not for environment settings.

objective.question: A learner runs this script in a fresh virtual environment where only `langchain` is installed. It fails on the `init_chat_model` line. What is the most likely cause and fix?

code.code:
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

load_dotenv()
model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5")
print(model.invoke("Hi").content)

options: The provider integration is missing; install `langchain-anthropic` in the same environment.
`load_dotenv()` must receive the path to .env explicitly or it raises an import error.
`init_chat_model` only works inside async code; switch to `await model.ainvoke("Hi")`.
The model string needs a `model_provider=` argument as well; add `model_provider="anthropic"`.
objective.explanation: `init_chat_model` imports the provider package at runtime. If `langchain-anthropic` is not installed, it raises an ImportError telling you to install it. The `provider:model` string is valid on its own, and `load_dotenv()` finds .env without a path.

objective.question: Your team uses uv. A developer runs the command below inside a project created with `uv init`. What does it do?

code.code: uv add langchain langchain-openai python-dotenv

options: It adds the packages to pyproject.toml, updates the uv.lock file and installs them into the project's virtual environment.
It only writes the packages to requirements.txt; you must run `uv sync` before anything is installed.
It installs the packages but does not record them anywhere, like a plain `pip install`.
It installs the packages globally for every Python on the machine.
objective.explanation: `uv add` records the dependencies in pyproject.toml, resolves and writes exact versions to uv.lock, and syncs the project environment (.venv). It never installs globally, and it does not use requirements.txt.

objective.question: This script raises an authentication error saying no API key was found, yet .env contains a valid ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. What is wrong?

code.code:
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from dotenv import load_dotenv

model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5")
load_dotenv()

print(model.invoke("Hello").content)

options: `init_chat_model` never reads environment variables; the key must be passed as `api_key=`.
The .env file must be named `.env.local` for python-dotenv to read it.
python-dotenv only works with OpenAI keys.
`load_dotenv()` runs after the model is created, so the key was not in the environment when the client was built.
objective.explanation: The chat model reads its key from the environment when it is created. Calling `load_dotenv()` first, at the top of the script, fixes the problem. The other options are false: chat models do read keys from the environment, python-dotenv works for any variable, and `.env` is the default file name.

objective.question: What happens when this code runs inside `async def main()`?

code.code:
async def main():
    response = model.ainvoke("Explain venv in one line")
    print(response.content)

options: It prints an empty string, because the call has not finished yet.
It raises an AttributeError, because `response` is a coroutine object and has no `.content`.
It raises a SyntaxError, because `ainvoke` cannot be called inside `async def`.
It prints the model's answer, because `ainvoke` blocks until it finishes.
objective.explanation: Without `await`, calling `ainvoke` only creates a coroutine; it does not run the model call. Reading `.content` on that coroutine raises an AttributeError, and Python also warns that the coroutine was never awaited.

objective.question: A learner runs `pip install langchain-anthropic` and it succeeds. Then `python app.py` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'langchain_anthropic'`. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Activate the project's virtual environment, then install with `python -m pip install langchain-anthropic` so pip uses the same interpreter that runs the script.
Add `langchain_anthropic` to the .env file so Python can find it.
Reinstall Python, because the standard library is corrupted.
Rename the import to `import langchain-anthropic` to match the package name.
objective.explanation: The `pip` command was probably linked to a different interpreter or environment than `python`. Running `python -m pip` inside the activated venv ties the install to the interpreter that runs the script. Hyphens are not valid in Python import names, and .env holds settings, not modules.

objective.question: You want to log token usage for each call. After `response = model.invoke("Hi")`, where does LangChain expose standardised token counts across providers?
options: `response.content["tokens"]`
`model.last_usage`, set on the chat model after each call
`response.tool_calls[0]["usage"]`
`response.usage_metadata`, with keys such as `input_tokens`, `output_tokens` and `total_tokens`
objective.explanation: AIMessage has a standard `usage_metadata` field that holds input, output and total token counts when the provider returns them. `content` holds the generated output, `tool_calls` holds requested tool invocations, and chat models have no `last_usage` attribute.

objective.question: In the code below, the third prompt hits a provider rate-limit error. The other four calls succeed. What is in `results`?

code.code:
import asyncio

async def main():
    prompts = ["p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5"]
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        *(model.ainvoke(p) for p in prompts),
        return_exceptions=True,
    )
    return results

results = asyncio.run(main())

options: Nothing; `gather` re-raises the rate-limit error and `results` is never assigned.
Five items in completion order, with the exception last.
Five items in the same order as `prompts`; index 2 holds the exception object and the rest are AIMessage objects.
Four AIMessage objects only; the failed call is dropped from the list.
objective.explanation: `gather` always returns results in the order the awaitables were passed in, not the order they finished. With `return_exceptions=True`, a failure is placed in its slot as an exception object instead of being raised. Without that flag, the first exception would propagate to the caller.

subjective.question: Why should every LangChain project use its own virtual environment? Explain how you create and activate one.
subjective.answer: A virtual environment gives each project its own Python interpreter and package set. LangChain and provider packages update often, so one project may need a newer version than another. Without isolation, an upgrade for one project can break another, and global installs are hard to reproduce. I create one inside the project with `python -m venv .venv`. On macOS or Linux I activate it with `source .venv/bin/activate`, and on Windows with `.venv\Scripts\activate`. After activation, `python` and `pip` point to the .venv folder, so `pip install -U langchain langchain-anthropic python-dotenv` installs only for this project. I add .venv to .gitignore and record dependencies in a requirements file or pyproject.toml so teammates can rebuild the same environment.
keyPoints: Isolates package versions per project
python -m venv .venv creates it
Activation differs on macOS/Linux vs Windows
Keep .venv out of Git; record dependencies instead

subjective.question: What is uv, and why might a team choose it over plain venv and pip?
subjective.answer: uv is a fast Python package and project manager from Astral. It can create virtual environments, install packages, and manage project dependencies with a lock file. Teams choose it mainly for speed, since installs and dependency resolution are much faster than pip, which helps in CI and when rebuilding environments often. It also combines several tools in one, so you can run `uv venv` to create an environment and `uv pip install` or `uv add` to add packages, and a lock file makes builds reproducible across machines. The ideas stay the same as venv: one isolated environment per project, dependencies declared in files, and secrets kept out of the code. For this course either tool works. What matters is that you use Python 3.10 or newer and an isolated environment.
keyPoints: uv is a fast package and project manager
Creates environments and installs packages
Lock file gives reproducible installs
Same isolation concept as venv

subjective.question: Explain the difference between the langchain package and a provider package such as langchain-anthropic.
subjective.answer: The langchain package holds the framework itself: the shared abstractions, message types, helpers like init_chat_model, and agent building with create_agent. It does not include the client code for every model vendor. Provider packages, such as langchain-anthropic or langchain-openai, contain the integration for one vendor, for example the ChatAnthropic or ChatOpenAI class and the vendor SDK dependency. This split keeps installs small and lets each integration be released on its own schedule. In practice you always install the core plus at least one provider: `pip install -U langchain langchain-anthropic`. If you call init_chat_model for a provider whose package is not installed, it fails with an import error. So the provider package decides which models you can actually reach.
keyPoints: Core langchain holds abstractions and agent APIs
Provider packages hold vendor-specific chat model classes
Split keeps installs light and versioned separately
Need core plus at least one provider

subjective.question: Walk through how you keep API keys secure in a Python AI project from day one.
subjective.answer: First, I never write a key in source code, notebooks or commit messages. I create a .env file in the project root with lines like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... and later LANGSMITH_API_KEY=... and LANGSMITH_TRACING=true. I add .env to .gitignore before the first commit. I commit a .env.example with the same names and empty values, so teammates know what to fill in. In code I call load_dotenv() from python-dotenv at the start of the entry script. The provider classes then read the standard variable names from the environment automatically, so I do not pass api_key at all. In production or CI I set the same variables through the platform's secret store instead of a file. If a key is ever leaked, I rotate it at the provider straight away, because removing it from Git history alone is not enough.
keyPoints: Keys in .env, never in code
Add .env to .gitignore; commit .env.example
load_dotenv() plus standard variable names
Use a secret store in production; rotate leaked keys

subjective.question: A colleague's script keeps using an expired key even after they updated .env. What is the likely cause and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The likely cause is that the old key is already set in the shell or system environment, for example from an earlier export or a profile file. By default load_dotenv() does not overwrite variables that already exist in the environment, so the old value wins and the new .env value is ignored. To confirm, I would run echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on macOS/Linux or check the variable in PowerShell, or print only whether os.environ has it and its last few characters, never the full key. The clean fix is to unset or update the old shell variable so there is one source of truth. If the team really wants the file to win, they can call load_dotenv(override=True), but they should do this on purpose, because it can also override values set by CI or production.
keyPoints: Existing environment variable takes priority
load_dotenv() does not override by default
Check the shell variable safely without printing the key
Unset it or use override=True deliberately

subjective.question: Write and explain a minimal script that calls a chat model and prints the response.
subjective.answer: My script has four parts. First, `from dotenv import load_dotenv` and `load_dotenv()`, which puts ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from .env into the environment. Second, `from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model` and `model = init_chat_model("anthropic:<model-name>")`, using a current model name from the provider's docs. Third, `response = model.invoke("Explain a virtual environment in one sentence.")`. Fourth, `print(response.content)`. The call returns an AIMessage, not a string, so .content gives the text. There is no api_key argument because the provider class reads the standard environment variable itself. I run it with the venv activated, using `python main.py`. If it fails, I check three things: the venv is active, langchain-anthropic is installed, and the key variable is set. This script is the base for every later step.
keyPoints: load_dotenv() first
init_chat_model with provider and model
invoke returns AIMessage; print .content
No hard-coded key; check venv, package and variable on failure

subjective.question: What does init_chat_model give you compared with importing ChatAnthropic directly?
subjective.answer: init_chat_model is a factory in langchain.chat_models that builds a chat model from a model identifier, such as a 'provider:model' string, or a model name plus model_provider. The main benefit is portability. My code depends on the common chat model interface, so switching from Anthropic to OpenAI is a change to one string or a config value, as long as the provider package is installed and the key is set. It also makes it easy to read the model name from an environment variable, which helps with testing and cost control. Importing ChatAnthropic directly is still fine when I need provider-specific options and know I will stay with one vendor. Either way, the returned object supports the same methods, such as invoke, ainvoke and stream, and returns AIMessage objects.
keyPoints: Factory that builds a model from a provider/model identifier
Makes switching providers a config change
Still needs the provider package and key
Same interface: invoke, ainvoke, stream

subjective.question: Describe the AIMessage object. Why should you not treat a model response as a plain string?
subjective.answer: When a chat model runs, it returns an AIMessage, which is LangChain's message type for model output. The text you usually want is in .content. But the object holds more than text. It can include tool calls the model wants to make, response metadata such as the model name and stop reason, and usage information like token counts when the provider reports them. For some providers, content can be a list of content blocks instead of one string, so code that assumes a string can break. Treating the response as a message also matters later. Agents and LangGraph keep a list of messages as state, and the AIMessage goes straight back into that history. So in my first script I print response.content, but I keep the full object for logging, debugging and passing to the next step.
keyPoints: Model calls return AIMessage
Text is in .content
Also carries tool calls, metadata, token usage
Content may be blocks; messages become agent state

subjective.question: Explain asyncio.run() and await. When would you use each in an AI project?
subjective.answer: asyncio.run(main()) creates an event loop, runs the coroutine main until it finishes, and then closes the loop. You call it once, at the entry point of a normal script. Inside async functions you use await to pause on a coroutine, such as `await model.ainvoke(prompt)`, so the loop can do other work while waiting for the network. The key rule is never to call asyncio.run() inside a loop that is already running. Jupyter notebooks, many web frameworks and some servers already run a loop. In a notebook cell you simply write `await main()`, and in a FastAPI route you make the handler async and await the call. Calling asyncio.run() there raises a RuntimeError. So: asyncio.run at the top level of scripts, await everywhere inside async code.
keyPoints: asyncio.run starts and closes one event loop
Call it once at the script entry point
await pauses on coroutines like ainvoke
In Jupyter or async frameworks, await directly

subjective.question: Why does async matter for LLM applications? Show how you would run several model calls concurrently.
subjective.answer: An LLM call spends most of its time waiting on the network for the provider. With sync invoke, the program sits idle during that wait, so ten calls take roughly ten times as long as one. With async, the event loop can start other calls while one is waiting. That is why web servers and agents that call many tools prefer ainvoke. To run calls concurrently, I write `async def main(): results = await asyncio.gather(*(model.ainvoke(p) for p in prompts))`, then loop over results and print each .content, and start it with asyncio.run(main()). Total time is closer to the slowest single call. I watch provider rate limits, though. For large batches I limit concurrency, for example with an asyncio.Semaphore, and I handle exceptions so one failed call does not hide the others.
keyPoints: LLM calls are I/O-bound network waits
ainvoke frees the loop while waiting
asyncio.gather runs calls concurrently
Respect rate limits; cap concurrency and handle errors

subjective.question: Your first script fails with an authentication error from the provider. How do you debug it step by step without exposing the key?
subjective.answer: I work from the outside in. First, I confirm the venv is active and the right provider package is installed, for example with pip show langchain-anthropic. Second, I check the .env file is in the folder I run from and that the variable name is exactly the standard one, such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, with no quotes problems or extra spaces. Third, I confirm load_dotenv() runs before the model is created. Fourth, I check whether an old value in the shell is overriding the file, because load_dotenv does not override by default. To inspect safely, I print only whether the variable exists and its length or last four characters, never the full key, and I never paste it into a chat or log. Finally, I check the key is active and has credit in the provider console, and rotate it if it might have leaked.
keyPoints: Check venv and provider package
Check .env location and exact variable name
load_dotenv before model creation; watch shell overrides
Inspect safely; verify key status in provider console

subjective.question: How does this week's setup prepare you for LangSmith tracing and later agent work?
subjective.answer: Everything later in the course builds on this base. LangSmith tracing is switched on purely by environment variables, LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, so with a working .env and load_dotenv() I can turn tracing on without touching code. The provider package and init_chat_model give me the model object that create_agent from langchain.agents will accept later. Understanding that a call returns an AIMessage helps me read agent state, which is a list of messages, and read traces. Async basics matter because agents and LangGraph graphs support async execution, and servers run them inside an event loop. Finally, the habit of an isolated environment with recorded dependencies makes it easy to deploy or share a project, and keeping secrets out of Git protects keys when I publish a repo or demo.
keyPoints: Tracing is enabled by env variables in .env
Model object feeds into create_agent
AIMessage knowledge helps read agent state and traces
Async and clean environments support deployment

subjective.question: A developer accidentally pushed a commit containing a .env file with a live OpenAI key to a public GitHub repository. They deleted the file in the next commit. Is the problem solved? Describe the full response.
subjective.answer: No. Deleting the file in a later commit leaves the key in Git history, and bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. The first step is to treat the key as compromised: revoke or rotate it in the provider console right away, and create a new key. Then check the provider's usage and billing dashboard for unexpected calls. Next, put the new key only in the local .env file and make sure `.env` is listed in .gitignore. Commit a `.env.example` file that contains variable names only. If the repository must stay clean, rewrite the history with a tool such as git filter-repo and force-push, but rotation is what actually removes the risk. Finally, prevent a repeat. Turn on GitHub secret scanning and push protection, or add a pre-commit secret scanner, so a key is blocked before it ever leaves the laptop.
keyPoints: Deleting the file does not remove the key from Git history
Revoke or rotate the key immediately and check usage
Add .env to .gitignore and share names only through .env.example
Use secret scanning or pre-commit hooks to stop future leaks

subjective.question: Two teammates run the same LangChain project. One gets a working app; the other gets import errors because a different langchain version was installed. How do you make the environment reproducible with pip or with uv?
subjective.answer: The cause is unpinned dependencies. Running `pip install langchain` picks whatever version is newest that day, so two people can end up with different versions. With pip, I create a venv, install the packages, and freeze exact versions with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`. Teammates then run `pip install -r requirements.txt` in their own venv. With uv, I declare dependencies with `uv add`, which writes them to pyproject.toml and records exact resolved versions in uv.lock. Both files are committed, and a teammate runs `uv sync` to get an identical environment. In both cases I also pin the Python version, for example 3.10 or later, using a `.python-version` file or `requires-python` in pyproject.toml. Upgrades become deliberate: one person bumps a version, tests the app, and commits the new lock file. This matters a lot in the LangChain ecosystem, because core packages and provider packages are released separately.
keyPoints: Unpinned installs pull different versions over time
pip: pip freeze into requirements.txt, then install -r
uv: pyproject.toml plus a committed uv.lock, then uv sync
Pin the Python version and upgrade on purpose

subjective.question: What does this startup code do, and why is it better than calling os.getenv inside the code that builds the model?

code.code:
import os
import sys
from dotenv import load_dotenv

REQUIRED = ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]

def load_config() -> None:
    load_dotenv()
    missing = [name for name in REQUIRED if not os.environ.get(name)]
    if missing:
        sys.exit(f"Missing environment variables: {', '.join(missing)}")

load_config()

subjective.answer: This code loads .env into the process environment. It then checks that each required variable exists and is not empty. If any are missing, it exits with a clear message that names the missing variables but never prints their values. This is a fail-fast pattern. Without it, a missing key shows up later as a confusing provider authentication error, or as a `None` value passed deep into the code, and that wastes debugging time. Because the check runs at startup, the problem appears before any model call is made, and the error message is the same on every machine and in CI. The list also documents what the app needs, which keeps it aligned with `.env.example`. It meets the step checkpoint: keys come from the environment, nothing is hard-coded, and the error output leaks no secrets. Later you can add LANGSMITH_API_KEY to REQUIRED when you turn on tracing.
keyPoints: Loads .env, then checks that required variables exist and are not empty
Fails fast with a clear message instead of a vague auth error later
Names the missing variables but never prints their values
Documents the app's needs and extends easily to LangSmith keys

subjective.question: You need to run 500 prompts through a chat model. Firing them all at once with asyncio.gather causes 429 rate-limit errors. How do you control concurrency?
subjective.answer: Unbounded `gather` opens 500 requests at once, and the provider's rate limits reject many of them. I would cap the number of calls running at the same time. The simplest LangChain way is to use batch with a config: `await model.abatch(prompts, config={"max_concurrency": 10})`. The sync version is `model.batch(...)`. Both keep results in input order. If I need custom logic, I wrap each call in an `asyncio.Semaphore(10)` and use `async with sem:` before the `ainvoke` call, then gather everything. I also pass `return_exceptions=True` so one failure does not cancel the whole run. Then I retry only the failed items, with backoff. Many chat model classes also accept a `max_retries` setting for transient errors. I tune the concurrency number against the provider's published limits for my account and watch token usage, because tokens per minute often runs out before requests per minute.
keyPoints: Unbounded gather overwhelms provider rate limits
Use abatch or batch with max_concurrency in the config
Or wrap ainvoke calls in an asyncio.Semaphore
Handle failures with return_exceptions and retries with backoff

subjective.question: Your local project uses a .env file. The team now wants to deploy the script in a Docker container on a cloud server. How should API keys be handled in production?
subjective.answer: .env is a local development convenience, not a production secret store. First, I keep `.env` out of the image by adding it to .dockerignore as well as .gitignore. Anyone who can pull an image can read files baked into it, including its layers. In production I inject the keys as real environment variables at runtime. Ideally they come from the platform's secret manager, such as a cloud secret manager, Kubernetes Secrets or the hosting platform's secret settings. My code does not need to change. `load_dotenv()` simply finds no file, the variables are already set, and by default load_dotenv does not override existing values. The provider classes read keys from the environment either way. I also use separate keys for dev and prod with limited permissions or budgets, rotate them regularly, and never log them. The fail-fast startup check still runs, so a misconfigured deployment stops immediately with a clear error.
keyPoints: Never bake .env into an image; add it to .dockerignore
Inject secrets at runtime as environment variables from a secret manager
Same code works because load_dotenv does not override existing values
Separate dev and prod keys, rotate them, never log them

subjective.question: Explain what this code does and how its output differs from calling ainvoke.

code.code:
import asyncio
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

load_dotenv()
model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-4.1")

async def main():
    async for chunk in model.astream("Explain asyncio in three lines"):
        print(chunk.content, end="", flush=True)
    print()

asyncio.run(main())

subjective.answer: The script first loads keys from .env and then builds an OpenAI chat model through init_chat_model. Inside an async function, it calls astream, which returns an async iterator, and loops over it with `async for`. Each item is an AIMessageChunk that holds a small piece of the reply. The script prints each piece as it arrives. Using `end=""` keeps the pieces on one line, and `flush=True` makes them appear on screen immediately. `asyncio.run(main())` starts the event loop, because this is a standalone script. With ainvoke, you wait for the full reply and get one complete AIMessage. With astream, you see tokens progressively, which makes the app feel faster in chat interfaces even though the total time is similar. If you need the full message as well, AIMessageChunk objects can be added together with `+` to build it up. The same streaming idea appears later when you drive LangGraph agents with stream events.
keyPoints: astream returns an async iterator of AIMessageChunk objects
async for plus print with end and flush shows text as it arrives
ainvoke waits and returns one complete AIMessage
Chunks can be added with + to rebuild the full message

subjective.question: A teammate wraps a chat model in an async web endpoint but calls model.invoke() inside `async def`. Under load, every request slows down. Explain why and how to fix it.

code.code:
async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    response = model.invoke(question)
    return response.content

subjective.answer: An async server runs many requests on one event loop. That works only if every handler gives control back to the loop while it waits. `invoke` is a blocking, synchronous network call, so while one request waits seconds for the LLM, the whole loop is frozen and every other request queues behind it. Throughput drops to roughly one model call at a time. The fix is `response = await model.ainvoke(question)`. While the network call is waiting, the loop is free to serve other requests, so many LLM calls overlap. Every LangChain chat model supports ainvoke, astream and abatch. If some library only offers a blocking call, run it with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so it does not block the loop. As a rule, inside `async def` use the `a`-prefixed methods, and in plain sync code use invoke. Do not call `asyncio.run` inside a running loop.
keyPoints: invoke blocks the event loop inside async code
All other requests wait behind the blocking call
Use await model.ainvoke so calls overlap
Use asyncio.to_thread for unavoidable blocking code

steps.overview: This step covers the core LangChain v1 building blocks that every agent uses: chat models, the four message types, prompt templates, structured output with Pydantic, and token streaming. These blocks appear inside every create_agent and LangGraph node later on the path. Getting reliable, schema-valid output here is the foundation for the tracing and evaluation work in LangSmith.
objectives: Initialise a chat model with init_chat_model and call it with invoke, batch and stream
Build conversations from SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage and ToolMessage objects
Create reusable prompts with ChatPromptTemplate and MessagesPlaceholder
Extract typed data into Pydantic models using with_structured_output and handle parsing failures
Stream tokens from a model and assemble AIMessageChunk objects into a full message

concepts.explanation: A chat model takes a list of messages and returns an AIMessage. init_chat_model("provider:model-name") from langchain.chat_models gives one interface across providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Ollama. Every chat model is a Runnable, so it supports invoke, batch, stream and their async forms (ainvoke, abatch, astream).

SystemMessage sets behaviour and rules. HumanMessage carries user input. AIMessage is the model reply and may contain tool_calls. ToolMessage returns a tool result to the model and must carry the matching tool_call_id.

In LangChain v1 a message exposes content_blocks, a provider-neutral list of typed blocks such as text, reasoning and tool calls. AIMessage also carries usage_metadata with input and output token counts. Use these instead of parsing raw provider responses.

ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", ...), ("human", "{email}")]) builds a prompt with named variables in curly braces. Calling invoke({"email": text}) fills the variables and returns a prompt value of messages. You pipe it into a model with the | operator to form a chain.

MessagesPlaceholder("history") inserts a whole list of messages at a position in the template. Use it for chat history or few-shot example messages. The variable you pass must be a list of message objects.

model.with_structured_output(MyModel) returns a Runnable whose output is a validated MyModel instance. Field names, types and Field(description=...) text become the schema the model sees, so good descriptions improve accuracy. Under the hood the provider uses tool calling or native JSON schema mode.

with_structured_output(MyModel, include_raw=True) returns a dict with raw (the AIMessage), parsed (the Pydantic object or None) and parsing_error. This lets you log or retry failures instead of crashing a batch job. It is the right pattern for the 10-email checkpoint.

model.stream(messages) yields AIMessageChunk objects as tokens arrive, which cuts perceived latency in UIs. Chunks can be added with + to build the final message. For agents built with create_agent you stream with stream_mode="messages" for tokens or "updates" for step-level progress.

keyFacts: init_chat_model uses the "provider:model" string format, for example "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5" or "ollama:llama3.1".
Messages live in langchain.messages in v1 (also importable from langchain_core.messages).
A ToolMessage without the correct tool_call_id breaks the tool-calling loop.
Prompt templates import from langchain_core.prompts; variables use {name} syntax and literal braces must be doubled {{ }}.
with_structured_output accepts a Pydantic model, TypedDict or JSON schema; only Pydantic gives you a validated object with attribute access.
Pydantic Optional fields with defaults let the model return null when data is missing instead of inventing values.
batch(inputs, config={"max_concurrency": 5}) processes many inputs in parallel with a concurrency cap.
In create_agent, pass response_format=MyModel to get a validated object in result["structured_response"].
Set temperature=0 for extraction tasks to make output more repeatable.

example.caption: Extract name, company and intent from emails into Pydantic objects
example.code:
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

class EmailInfo(BaseModel):
    name: Optional[str] = Field(None, description="Sender's full name, null if absent")
    company: Optional[str] = Field(None, description="Sender's company, null if absent")
    intent: Literal["sales_inquiry", "support", "complaint", "partnership", "other"]

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "Extract sender details. Never guess missing values."),
    ("human", "Email:\n{email}"),
])
model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", temperature=0)
chain = prompt | model.with_structured_output(EmailInfo, include_raw=True)

emails = ["Hi, I'm Priya Nair from Zoho. Can we discuss bulk pricing?",
          "Order 4411 arrived broken. - Rahul"]  # extend to 10

results = chain.batch([{"email": e} for e in emails], config={"max_concurrency": 5})
for e, r in zip(emails, results):
    if r["parsing_error"] or r["parsed"] is None:
        print("FAILED:", e[:40], r["parsing_error"])
    else:
        EmailInfo.model_validate(r["parsed"].model_dump())  # checkpoint check
        print(r["parsed"])

for chunk in model.stream("Summarise these emails in one line."):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)

pitfalls: Making every field required: the model then invents a company or name. Use Optional with a default of None.
Using a free-text intent field: results become inconsistent. Use Literal or an Enum so validation enforces allowed values.
Forgetting that with_structured_output without include_raw raises on parse failure and can stop a whole batch.
Mixing old APIs such as LLMChain, initialize_agent or create_react_agent from older tutorials instead of LCEL pipes and create_agent in v1.
Streaming a with_structured_output chain and expecting token text; it streams partial structures, not plain tokens.
Passing a plain string where MessagesPlaceholder expects a list of messages.

# email-lead-extractor (Step 2: LangChain building blocks)

Extract `name`, `company` and `intent` from 10 emails into Pydantic objects.

## Files
- `app/schema.py` - the `EmailLead` Pydantic model (the contract).
- `app/prompts.py` - `ChatPromptTemplate`, `MessagesPlaceholder`, few-shot messages.
- `app/extract.py` - hands-on task: batch extraction plus the checkpoint.
- `app/stream_demo.py` - system/human/AI/tool messages, token streaming,
  `content_blocks`, `usage_metadata` and `response_metadata`.
- `data/emails.json` - the 10 input emails.

## Setup
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
export MODEL=openai:gpt-4.1-mini   # any "provider:model" string works
```
To use another provider, install its package (for example
`langchain-anthropic`) and change `MODEL`, e.g. `anthropic:<model-name>`.

## Run
```bash
python -m app.extract       # hands-on task + checkpoint
python -m app.stream_demo   # streaming and message types
```

## Checkpoint
`app.extract` prints `10/10 results validated` and exits with code 0.
Any parsing error (from `include_raw=True`) or Pydantic `ValidationError`
is printed with the email id, and the script exits with code 1.

## Key ideas to remember
- `init_chat_model("provider:model")` gives one interface for all providers.
- `prompt | model.with_structured_output(Schema)` returns a Pydantic object.
- `include_raw=True` returns a dict: `raw`, `parsed`, `parsing_error`.
- `model.stream(...)` yields `AIMessageChunk`s; add them to get the full message.

# LangChain v1 family (current major versions)
langchain>=1.0,<2.0
langchain-core>=1.0,<2.0
# Provider integration used by init_chat_model("openai:...")
langchain-openai>=1.0,<2.0
# Pydantic v2 is required for with_structured_output schemas
pydantic>=2.7,<3.0
# Optional: tracing in LangSmith (used later in Step 5)
# export LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY=... to enable
langsmith>=0.4

"""Pydantic schema: the contract every extraction must satisfy."""
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# A closed set of labels makes results easy to route and to evaluate.
Intent = Literal[
    "sales_inquiry",
    "support_request",
    "partnership",
    "job_application",
    "complaint",
    "other",
]


class EmailLead(BaseModel):
    """Structured facts extracted from one inbound email."""

    # Field descriptions are sent to the model as part of the JSON schema,
    # so write them as instructions.
    name: str | None = Field(
        description="Sender's full name as written in the email, or null if not stated."
    )
    company: str | None = Field(
        description="Sender's company or organisation, or null if not stated."
    )
    intent: Intent = Field(description="The main reason the sender wrote the email.")
    summary: str = Field(
        max_length=200,  # Pydantic enforces this when the result is validated
        description="One-sentence summary of the request, under 200 characters.",
    )

"""Prompt templates and few-shot messages shared by both scripts."""
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder

EXTRACT_SYSTEM = (
    "You extract contact details and intent from business emails. "
    "Use only facts stated in the email. If a name or company is missing, return null. "
    "Choose exactly one intent label."
)

# ChatPromptTemplate turns variables into a list of messages.
EXTRACT_PROMPT = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        ("system", EXTRACT_SYSTEM),
        # MessagesPlaceholder injects a whole list of messages (few-shot here).
        MessagesPlaceholder("examples", optional=True),
        ("human", "Email:\n{email}"),
    ]
)

# One worked example as a human/AI message pair.
FEW_SHOT = [
    HumanMessage("Email:\nHi, Meera from Zylo Foods here. Our invoice portal shows a 500 error."),
    AIMessage(
        'name="Meera", company="Zylo Foods", intent="support_request", '
        'summary="Invoice portal returns a 500 error."'
    ),
]

# Prompt for the streaming demo: history can hold AI and tool messages.
REPLY_PROMPT = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
    [
        ("system", "You are a polite sales assistant. Reply in under 80 words."),
        MessagesPlaceholder("history"),
        ("human", "{request}"),
    ]
)

"""Hands-on task: extract EmailLead objects from 10 emails and validate all."""
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from pydantic import ValidationError

from app.prompts import EXTRACT_PROMPT, FEW_SHOT
from app.schema import EmailLead

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "openai:gpt-4.1-mini")
DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "emails.json"


def main() -> int:
    # One call works for any provider: "provider:model".
    model = init_chat_model(MODEL, temperature=0)
    # include_raw=True -> {"raw": AIMessage, "parsed": EmailLead | None, "parsing_error": ...}
    structured = model.with_structured_output(EmailLead, include_raw=True)
    chain = EXTRACT_PROMPT | structured  # LCEL: prompt output feeds the model

    emails = json.loads(DATA.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    inputs = [{"email": e["body"], "examples": FEW_SHOT} for e in emails]
    results = chain.batch(inputs, config={"max_concurrency": 5})  # parallel calls

    passed = 0
    for email, res in zip(emails, results):
        if res["parsing_error"] is not None or res["parsed"] is None:
            print(f"[FAIL] {email['id']}: {res['parsing_error']}")
            continue
        try:
            # Checkpoint: re-validate so max_length and Literal rules are enforced.
            lead = EmailLead.model_validate(res["parsed"].model_dump())
        except ValidationError as err:
            print(f"[FAIL] {email['id']}: {err}")
            continue
        passed += 1
        tokens = (res["raw"].usage_metadata or {}).get("total_tokens")
        print(f"[OK] {email['id']} tokens={tokens} -> {lead.model_dump_json()}")

    print(f"\n{passed}/{len(emails)} results validated")
    return 0 if passed == len(emails) else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

"""Message types, token streaming, content blocks and metadata."""
import os

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage, ToolMessage

from app.prompts import REPLY_PROMPT

MODEL = os.getenv("MODEL", "openai:gpt-4.1-mini")

# History with human, AI (tool call) and tool messages. The system message
# comes from REPLY_PROMPT. Each ToolMessage must match a tool_call id.
HISTORY = [
    HumanMessage("Email: Hi, I am Arjun Rao from Kavya Textiles. Please share pricing for 50 seats."),
    AIMessage(
        content="",
        tool_calls=[{"name": "crm_lookup", "args": {"company": "Kavya Textiles"},
                     "id": "call_1", "type": "tool_call"}],
    ),
    ToolMessage("Kavya Textiles: new lead, region=South India, no open deals.", tool_call_id="call_1"),
]


def main() -> None:
    # stream_usage=True asks OpenAI to send token usage in the final chunk.
    model = init_chat_model(MODEL, temperature=0.3, stream_usage=True)
    messages = REPLY_PROMPT.invoke(
        {"history": HISTORY, "request": "Draft a reply to Arjun."}
    ).to_messages()
    for m in messages:
        print(f"{m.type:>6}: {str(m.content)[:60]}")  # system, human, ai, tool

    print("\n--- streaming ---")
    full = None
    for chunk in model.stream(messages):  # yields AIMessageChunk objects
        print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)  # .text is the plain-text part
        full = chunk if full is None else full + chunk  # chunks add up

    print("\n\n--- final message ---")
    print("content_blocks:", full.content_blocks)  # provider-neutral blocks
    print("usage_metadata:", full.usage_metadata)  # input/output/total tokens
    print("response_metadata:", full.response_metadata)  # model name, finish reason


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
