options: Remove the checkpointer, because checkpointers need a conditional edge.
Rename the node "retrieve" to "__start__".
Call graph.invoke with {"configurable": {"entry": "retrieve"}}.
Add builder.add_edge(START, "retrieve") so the graph knows where to begin.
objective.explanation: A StateGraph needs an edge from START to define where execution begins. The checkpointer is unrelated, renaming nodes to reserved names is wrong, and no entry key exists in the config.

objective.question: In LangSmith traces, your agent answers policy questions from its own knowledge and never calls the RAG tool below. What is the most likely cause?
options: The @tool decorator only works on async functions.
RAG tools must be passed through middleware, not through the tools list.
Tools that return strings are ignored by create_agent.
The tool name and docstring are too vague, so the model cannot tell when to use it. Give it a clear name and a description of what it searches and when to call it.
objective.explanation: The model chooses tools from their names, descriptions and arguments. A clear name like search_hr_policies, a useful docstring and a system prompt that says when to search usually fix this. The other options describe restrictions that do not exist.

objective.question: During evaluation runs, one example makes your agent loop between the model and a failing tool, and token costs spike. Which change addresses this most directly with LangChain v1 built-ins?
options: Remove the checkpointer so the loop cannot save state.
Turn off LANGSMITH_TRACING to reduce token usage.
Increase the SummarizationMiddleware trigger so the loop has more context.
Add the built-in model call limit middleware (and tool retry middleware with sensible retries) so a run stops after a bounded number of model calls.
objective.explanation: LangChain v1 ships middleware for model call limits and tool retry, which bound runaway loops. Removing persistence or tracing does not stop the loop, and more context does not fix a failing tool.

objective.question: You deploy your capstone on the Agent Server. Your code still compiles the graph with checkpointer=InMemorySaver(). What should you do?
options: Keep InMemorySaver, because the Agent Server has no persistence of its own.
Replace thread_id with a user_id, because the Agent Server ignores threads.
Move the checkpointer onto each subagent instead of the main agent.
Rely on the Agent Server, which handles persistence automatically, and do not hard-code an in-memory checkpointer for deployment.
objective.explanation: The Agent Server provides persistence, so an in-memory saver is only for local development and would lose state on restart. Threads are still used, and only the outermost graph should carry persistence.

subjective.question: Walk me through the architecture of your capstone agent.
subjective.answer: My capstone is a support agent built with create_agent from langchain.agents, which returns a compiled LangGraph graph. It has three tools. A retrieve_docs tool runs RAG over a vector store of product docs. A lookup_order tool reads order data. A send_email tool takes action. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware guards send_email, so a person can approve, edit or reject each email before it goes out. SummarizationMiddleware keeps long threads within the context budget. The agent is compiled with a checkpointer, and every call passes a thread_id, so conversations persist and interrupts can resume. LANGSMITH_TRACING is on, so every run is traced. I also keep a LangSmith dataset of about 40 questions with reference answers. I run evaluate() against it with a correctness judge and a retrieval check, and I compare experiments whenever I change the prompt or the model. The README contains the diagram, the results and a demo link.
keyPoints: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph
RAG exposed as a tool alongside action tools
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on risky tools plus a checkpointer and thread_id
LangSmith tracing and an evaluation dataset with evaluate()

subjective.question: Why did you expose RAG as a tool instead of retrieving on every turn?
subjective.answer: Making retrieval a tool lets the model decide when it needs documents. Greetings, follow-ups that the conversation history already answers, and pure action requests skip retrieval. That cuts latency and cost, and it keeps irrelevant chunks out of the context, which can confuse the model. It also allows multi-step behaviour. The agent can retrieve, see the results are weak, and retrieve again with a refined query. The tool description matters a lot, so I state what the corpus contains and when to use it. The trade-off is that the model may skip retrieval when it should not. I watch for that in LangSmith traces, and my evaluation set includes questions that need grounding. If skipping shows up often, I tighten the system prompt or the tool description. For strict compliance use cases, an always-retrieve step in a custom LangGraph node is still a valid choice.
keyPoints: Model decides when to retrieve, which saves cost and latency
Enables iterative, multi-step retrieval
Tool description quality drives correct use
Risk of skipped retrieval is monitored with traces and evals

subjective.question: Explain the full human-approval flow in your agent, from the tool call to the resume.
subjective.answer: The model proposes a send_email tool call. Because send_email is listed in HumanInTheLoopMiddleware's interrupt_on, the middleware pauses the run before the tool executes. The checkpointer saves state under the current thread_id. I drive the graph with stream_events using version="v3", and the stream reports the interruption and its payload. That payload contains the proposed tool call and the allowed decisions, which are approve, edit and reject. My UI shows the email to the reviewer. When the reviewer decides, I call the agent again with Command(resume=...) carrying that decision, on the same thread_id. On approve, the tool runs as proposed. On edit, it runs with the reviewer's changed arguments. On reject, the tool does not run and the model receives that feedback. Without a checkpointer and a thread_id there is nothing to resume, so the checkpointer is mandatory.
keyPoints: interrupt_on with allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject
State saved by the checkpointer under thread_id
Interrupt surfaced through stream_events v3
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id

subjective.question: What exactly do the checkpointer and thread_id do, and how would this change in production?
subjective.answer: A checkpointer saves the graph's state at each step. thread_id is the key that groups those checkpoints into one conversation. I pass it as config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}}. Without it the checkpointer cannot save or resume anything. That breaks memory and also breaks human-in-the-loop, because an interrupt has nowhere to resume from. Checkpoints also enable debugging and time travel. graph.get_state_history(config) lists them newest first, so I can inspect the state at any step. In development I use InMemorySaver, which disappears when the process restarts. In production I would use a durable, database-backed checkpointer, or deploy on the Agent Server, which handles persistence automatically. A store such as InMemoryStore is different. It holds long-term memory shared across threads, while the checkpointer holds the state of each thread.
keyPoints: Checkpointer saves state per step and thread_id keys the conversation
No thread_id means no save, no resume and no HITL
get_state_history returns checkpoints newest first
InMemorySaver for dev; durable saver or Agent Server in production; store is cross-thread memory

subjective.question: An interrupted node re-runs from its start when resumed. What problems does this cause and how do you design for it?
subjective.answer: When I resume with Command(resume=...), LangGraph does not continue from the line after interrupt(). It re-runs the whole node, and on this second run interrupt() returns the resume value instead of pausing. Any code before the interrupt therefore runs twice. That includes API calls, database writes, charging a card or sending a notification. To design for this, I place interrupt() at the very top of the node, or I put side effects in a separate node after the approval node. If work must happen before the pause, I make it idempotent, for example with an idempotency key or an upsert. I also avoid expensive LLM calls before an interrupt, because they double the cost. If a node has several interrupts, I keep their order fixed, because resume values are matched by order. I test this by checking traces for duplicate tool spans after resume.
keyPoints: Resume re-runs the node from its start; interrupt() returns the resume value
Code before interrupt runs twice
Put interrupt first or move side effects to separate nodes
Make pre-interrupt work idempotent and keep the order of multiple interrupts stable

subjective.question: A user reports a wrong answer from your agent. How do you use LangSmith to find the cause?
subjective.answer: With LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set, every run is a trace. I find the run by filtering on thread_id metadata, time or user feedback. I open the trace tree and read it in order. First the model call: did it pick the right tool? Next the retrieve_docs span: what query was sent, and were the returned chunks relevant? Then the final model call: did it use the chunks or ignore them? This quickly shows whether the fault is retrieval, tool choice or generation. For deeper stepping, I run the agent locally with langgraph dev and open it in LangSmith Studio. I then add the failing case to my evaluation dataset with the correct reference answer, so the bug becomes a regression test. After the fix, I run evaluate() again and compare the new experiment with the old one.
keyPoints: Tracing via LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY
Inspect tool choice, retrieval and generation spans to localise the fault
Studio via langgraph dev and langgraph.json for interactive debugging
Add the failure to the dataset and re-run evaluate() to confirm the fix

subjective.question: How did you build the evaluation set for your capstone, and what does each example contain?
subjective.answer: I created a LangSmith dataset of about 40 examples. Each example has inputs, which are the user question, and reference outputs, which are the expected answer and sometimes the expected source document or tool. I covered several categories. There are common questions answerable from the docs, multi-step questions that need retrieval and an order lookup, out-of-scope questions where the right answer is 'I don't know', and adversarial or ambiguous prompts. I also added cases that should trigger send_email, to check that the agent proposes the action rather than doing it silently. I seeded examples from real traces and hand-wrote the edge cases. The dataset is versioned, so results stay comparable over time. I run evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]), where target wraps my agent. Every prompt or model change gets its own named experiment, so I can compare them side by side.
keyPoints: Dataset of examples with inputs and reference outputs
Coverage: happy path, multi-step, out-of-scope, adversarial, action cases
Seed from real traces and add hand-written edge cases
evaluate() creates comparable experiments per change

subjective.question: What are the risks of LLM-as-judge evaluation, and how did you mitigate them?
subjective.answer: I used create_llm_as_judge from openevals with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, comparing outputs to the reference answers. The judge is fast and handles paraphrases well, but it has known risks. It can be inconsistent across runs, it may favour long or confident answers, and it can share blind spots with the model it is judging. To mitigate this, I use a strong judge model and ask for a score with reasoning, so I can audit its decisions. I spot-check a sample of judgements by hand and fix the rubric when the judge and I disagree. I also pair the judge with deterministic code evaluators. Examples are whether the right tool was called, whether a source was cited, and whether out-of-scope questions were refused. These are cheap and exact. Finally, I track trends across experiments rather than trusting one absolute number.
keyPoints: create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT from openevals
Risks: inconsistency, length bias, shared blind spots
Human spot checks and rubric tuning
Combine with deterministic code evaluators and compare experiments

subjective.question: When would you add subagents to the capstone, and how would you structure them?
subjective.answer: I would add subagents when one agent has too many tools or the context becomes crowded. One example is a research worker that does many retrieval rounds, next to a drafting worker that writes emails. The current pattern is a main create_agent whose tools wrap worker subagents. Each worker is its own create_agent with a focused prompt and tool set. The wrapper tool invokes the worker and returns only its final result, which keeps the main agent's context clean. I would not use langgraph-supervisor, because it is no longer actively maintained. Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer, so persistence and interrupts are handled once, at the top. The workers do not get their own. For long-running, file-heavy tasks, create_deep_agent is an option, because it pre-assembles a filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching. For a demo, I keep it optional, because a single agent is easier to explain.
keyPoints: Use subagents when tools or context overload a single agent
Main create_agent with tools wrapping worker subagents
Do not use langgraph-supervisor; it is no longer actively maintained
Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; create_deep_agent for long tasks

subjective.question: What goes into your capstone README, and why does it matter in an interview?
subjective.answer: The README is my interview artefact, so a reviewer should understand the project in two minutes. It opens with the problem and a one-line summary. Next comes an architecture diagram showing the user, the create_agent graph, its middleware, the tools (RAG retriever, order lookup, send_email with human approval), the checkpointer and LangSmith. Then there are setup steps: the required environment variables, including LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, and how to run it with langgraph dev. The evaluation section names the dataset and its size, lists the evaluators, and shows a results table comparing at least two experiments. A design decisions section explains why RAG is a tool, how interrupt and resume work, and the known limitations. It ends with a demo link, either a short video or a hosted app, plus a sample trace screenshot. Evidence-backed numbers make interview answers credible and specific.
keyPoints: Problem statement and architecture diagram
Setup with env vars and the langgraph dev command
Evaluation results comparing experiments
Design decisions, limitations and a demo link

subjective.question: How does your UI drive the agent and detect that it is waiting for human approval?
subjective.answer: I drive the graph with stream_events(..., version="v3"), which is the recommended approach. It streams model tokens, tool start and end events, and state updates. I can therefore show the reply as it is generated, along with progress such as 'searching docs'. When HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses on send_email, the stream reports the interruption through stream.interrupted, and stream.interrupts holds the payload with the proposed action and the allowed decisions. The UI then switches to an approval card with approve, edit and reject buttons. The click sends Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, and streaming continues. Because state lives in the checkpointer, the reviewer does not have to answer immediately. The thread can resume later, even from another session, as long as the same thread_id is used and the checkpointer is durable.
keyPoints: stream_events with version="v3" is the recommended driver
stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts surface pauses
UI renders the approval and resumes with Command(resume=...)
Durable checkpointer allows a delayed resume on the same thread_id

subjective.question: How do you present your certificates and Langflow work honestly on your CV and in interviews?
subjective.answer: I list the LangChain Academy courses I completed: LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith. They are free, self-paced courses with notebooks and videos. I describe them as course completions, not professional certifications, and I back them with my capstone, because the project is the real proof. For Langflow, I say plainly that there is no official certification. Instead, I show a published flow that I built using the official docs and tutorials, for example a visual prototype of the same RAG assistant. I explain that I use Langflow to prototype and demo ideas quickly with components, test them in the Playground, and call the flow through its API. I then move to Python with create_agent and LangGraph when I need finer control, testing and evaluation. Interviewers value accuracy, so I never invent credentials.
keyPoints: LangChain Academy courses are free, self-paced and course-based
The capstone is the main proof of skill
Langflow has no official certification; show a published flow
Langflow for visual prototyping; Python LangGraph for production control

subjective.question: Explain what this agent setup does, step by step, and how you would test each part before your demo.

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import (
    SummarizationMiddleware, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, PIIMiddleware)
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    tools=[search_policies, send_email],
    system_prompt="Answer HR questions using search_policies. Cite sources.",
    middleware=[
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True),
        SummarizationMiddleware(model="openai:gpt-4.1-mini",
            trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20)),
        HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={
            "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}),
    ],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

subjective.answer: create_agent builds a compiled LangGraph agent that loops between the model and two tools. search_policies is the RAG tool. send_email is the risky action. PIIMiddleware redacts emails in the input before the model sees them. SummarizationMiddleware compresses old history once the thread passes about 4,000 tokens and keeps the last 20 messages. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses before every send_email call so a reviewer can approve, edit or reject it. InMemorySaver stores state per thread_id, which makes that pause and resume possible. To test it, I send an input with an email and check in the LangSmith trace that it is redacted. I run a long synthetic chat and confirm a summary appears. I trigger send_email and check the run interrupts, then resume with approve, edit and reject on the same thread_id. Finally, I run the evaluation dataset to confirm the answers still cite sources.
keyPoints: create_agent returns a compiled graph; the tools are RAG plus a risky action
PII redaction on input, and summarisation with token trigger and message keep
HITL interrupt on send_email with approve, edit and reject
Checkpointer plus thread_id enables pause and resume
A concrete test for each feature using traces and the evaluation set

subjective.question: Your RAG tool is being called, but answers are still wrong because the retrieved chunks are irrelevant. How do you diagnose and fix this?
subjective.answer: First I open the failing run in LangSmith and look at the tool span. It shows the exact query the model sent and the chunks that came back. That tells me whether the problem is the query, the retrieval or the generation. If the model rewrote the question badly, I improve the tool description and the system prompt, or I let the tool accept the user's wording. If the query is fine but the chunks are poor, I check chunk size and overlap, the embedding model, metadata filters and the k value. Often I need smaller chunks with section titles attached. If good chunks came back but the answer ignored them, it is a prompting or grounding issue. I add the failing cases to my LangSmith dataset. Then I separate retrieval checks, such as whether the expected source was retrieved, from answer correctness, and I re-run evaluate() after each change to confirm the fix.
keyPoints: Use the tool span in the trace to see the query and the returned chunks
Isolate the failure: query formulation, retrieval quality or generation
Fixes: chunking, embeddings, metadata filters, k, tool description
Add failures to the dataset and measure retrieval and answer quality separately
Re-run the experiment to confirm the improvement

subjective.question: A final-answer correctness score is not enough for a multi-step agent. What else would you evaluate in your capstone, and how?
subjective.answer: For a multi-step agent, the path matters as much as the answer. I add trajectory checks. Did the agent call the RAG tool when the question needed internal data? Did it avoid calling send_email when it should only answer? Did it stay within a reasonable number of steps? I write these as simple code evaluators that read the run's messages and tool calls, because deterministic checks are cheaper and more reliable than a judge. I keep LLM-as-judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT for answer quality against reference outputs. For human approval, I test that an interrupt happens for every risky tool call, and that a reject leads to a sensible reply instead of the action. I also track latency and token cost from the traces. All of these run as one evaluate() experiment, so I can compare versions side by side.
keyPoints: Trajectory checks: correct tool selection and no unwanted actions
Step-count, latency and cost from traces
Deterministic code evaluators where possible, LLM judge for answer quality
Verify interrupts fire for risky tools and that the reject path behaves well
Compare versions as experiments on the same dataset

subjective.question: The reviewer chooses "edit" or "reject" on a send_email call. What should your agent do in each case, and what bugs have you seen here?
subjective.answer: On approve, the tool runs with the original arguments. On edit, the reviewer's changed arguments replace the model's, such as a corrected recipient or body, and the tool runs with those. On reject, the tool does not run. The agent should get feedback that the action was declined and then tell the user, or ask what to change, instead of silently retrying. In every case I resume on the same thread_id. Common bugs include resuming on a new thread_id, which loses the paused state. Another is a UI that does not check for interrupts and shows the run as finished. A third is the model trying the same email again straight after a reject. Side effects placed before the pause can also run twice, because the node re-runs from its start on resume. I cover all three decisions in tests and confirm them in the LangSmith traces.
keyPoints: Approve runs the original call; edit runs with the reviewer's arguments; reject skips the tool
Always resume on the same thread_id
After a reject, the agent informs the user instead of retrying blindly
Watch for duplicate side effects because the node re-runs on resume
Test all three decisions and check the traces

subjective.question: Would you build your capstone with create_agent or create_deep_agent? Justify the choice.
subjective.answer: For my capstone I used create_agent. The task is bounded: answer questions with RAG, and send an email only after human approval. A single agent loop with a few middleware is easy to explain, trace and evaluate. create_deep_agent is meant for long-running, open-ended tasks. It pre-assembles a filesystem for intermediate work, summarisation, subagents and prompt caching. I would switch to it if the capstone grew into multi-hour research, such as reading many documents, writing drafts to files and delegating sections to subagents. That extra machinery adds behaviour I would need to understand and evaluate, so I avoid it when the task does not need it. In an interview, I explain that I picked the simplest design that met the requirements, and I describe the signals that would make me move to a deep agent.
keyPoints: create_agent suits bounded tasks and is easier to trace and evaluate
create_deep_agent bundles filesystem, summarisation, subagents and prompt caching
Switch for long-running, multi-file or delegated work
Avoid unnecessary complexity and justify the choice by requirements

subjective.question: You prototyped the agent visually in Langflow first. How do you move from that prototype to the Python capstone, and what do you show from Langflow?
subjective.answer: I used Langflow to try ideas quickly. I connected a loader, a vector store, a retriever and a model as components, then tested prompts in the Playground. This helped me choose the chunk settings, the prompt and the tool layout before I wrote any code. For the capstone, I rebuilt the logic in Python with create_agent, a retriever tool and HumanInTheLoopMiddleware. Code gives me version control, unit tests, checkpointers, LangSmith evaluation and a clean deployment path. I keep the Langflow flow as a separate artefact. I publish it or export it and call it through its API, and I link it from the README with a short note on what I learned from it. In interviews, I am clear that Langflow has no official certification. My evidence is the published flow and how I used it to make design decisions.
keyPoints: Langflow is for rapid visual prototyping with components and the Playground
Port the validated design into Python with create_agent and middleware
Python adds tests, version control, evaluation and deployment
Publish or share the flow and link it in the README
Be honest that Langflow has no official certification

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: "Your agent is slow and expensive. Use your traces to make it cheaper without losing quality." How do you answer?
subjective.answer: I start from data, not guesses. In LangSmith, I sort runs by latency and token usage and open the worst ones to see where time and tokens go. That might be long histories, large retrieved contexts, repeated tool calls or retries. Then I apply targeted fixes. SummarizationMiddleware keeps context small in long threads. I reduce k or chunk size in the RAG tool. I add the model call limit middleware to stop loops, and tool retry middleware with sane limits so failures do not cascade. I may use a cheaper model for summarisation, or model fallback middleware for resilience. For agents with many tools, the LLM tool selection middleware can shrink the tool list per call. After each change, I re-run evaluate() on the same dataset and compare experiments. That way I only keep changes that cut cost or latency while correctness stays at the same level.
keyPoints: Find the hotspots from trace latency and token data
Fixes: summarisation, a smaller retrieval context, call limits, tool retry
Cheaper models where suitable; tool selection for large toolsets
Validate every change with an evaluation experiment
Keep only changes that hold quality steady
